task_brief: Day 1 of "Programming Foundations: Data, Control, and Functions" (unit 2, grade 9) is a diagnostic probe on data types and type conversion. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Build a modular program that uses compound conditions, nested iteration, and composed functions to solve a stated problem for a real user. Today's work contributes to that by handling data types and type conversion at the launch and diagnostic stage, against the unit's wider topics of data types and type conversion, expressions operators and precedence, selection and compound boolean logic, and iteration nested loops and loop conditions. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Before any explanation of data types and type conversion, record what you already think. Write your current best answer to how data types and type conversion works, then sketch — in words, boxes, or pseudocode — the steps you believe are involved. Predict one input that would make your sketch fail. Then run or hand-trace your own sketch against two inputs you invent and mark where the prediction held and where it broke. Wrong predictions are the point of this task and cost you nothing; an unrecorded prediction is the only way to lose credit. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about data types and type conversion, and it belongs to "Programming Foundations: Data, Control, and Functions", which also covers separate topics such as expressions operators and precedence. Close out with this check before you stop: Name one thing you already understand about data types and type conversion and one thing you want resolved by the end of the unit. At grade 9 the bar is independent work with explicit criteria set before you start, and evidence that you evaluated the finished result against those criteria rather than against how it felt.

debugging_target.observed_failure: The selection is correct, but the aggregation subtracts each selected value, so the supplied records return -6 instead of 6.
debugging_target.target: Repair the aggregation operator, explain the selected rows and accumulator state, and rerun all three tests.
debugging_target.passing_change: The reducer uses total + record.value; the tests return 6, 0, and 0.
debugging_target.scope_note: Diagnosing the state, control-flow, or data defect and connecting the repair to data types and type conversion is the central evidence.

remediation: Reteaching for data types and type conversion follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for data types and type conversion, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to data types and type conversion works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of data types and type conversion, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking data types and type conversion mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
